title: Your practical DSA roadmap
subtitle: 11 connected stages. One clear next step.
intro: Data structures organize information; algorithms turn it into answers. This guide expands the eleven stages in your roadmap into an actual learning path. Use Python 3 for the examples, or translate the ideas into a language you already know. Progress by what you can explain and build, rather than a calendar deadline. The advanced stage is an optional menu, not a condition for being good at DSA.

foundations.title: Before stage 1: build your toolkit
foundations.intro: The picture begins with arrays, but these foundations make every later topic easier. If you already know them, use the checks to skip ahead.
tasks: Programming: write functions, loops and conditionals; use variables, lists, dictionaries and sets; understand return values, references and mutation. Run a small program and read an error message without guessing.

Complexity: define the input size n and count how work grows. Compare O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²) and exponential work. Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound, not a stopwatch. Distinguish worst-case, expected and amortized costs; include extra memory.

Sorting: trace insertion sort and understand why its worst case is quadratic. Use sorted() for a new Python list and list.sort() to change an existing one. After recursion, implement merge sort and explain its O(n log n) work and usual O(n) auxiliary space.

Hashing: use a set for membership and a dictionary for key–value lookup or counting. Understand collisions and hashable keys. Lookup is typically expected O(1), not a universal worst-case guarantee; hashing a long fresh string also takes work.

Reasoning: practice tiny hand-worked examples, simple invariants and a short correctness argument. An invariant is a fact that remains true as your loop runs, such as “everything before this index has already been counted.”
checks: Can you write a frequency counter and explain when a set loses information?
Can you explain why a nested loop is sometimes quadratic, but two consecutive loops are linear?
Can you test empty, singleton, duplicate and negative-value inputs?

firstSession: Write a function that returns the largest number in a nonempty list, without max(). Decide what your function should do for an empty list.
Trace it on [4, -2, 9, 9]. Write down what your “best so far” variable means after each step.
Add tests for one item, all-negative values and repeated maxima. Then explain its O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
studyTips: For each exercise: clarify the contract, make a tiny example, write a simple correct solution, then improve it.
Try independently before reading a hint. If you use a solution, close it and rebuild the idea later from a blank file.
Keep a short mistake log: the failing case, the broken assumption and the corrected invariant.
Mix a new problem with an older one. Being able to recognize and explain a pattern matters more than a solved-problem count.
Move on when you can explain the approach, implement it without copying and test edge cases. Revisit a topic whenever a later stage exposes a gap.

stages.title: Arrays
stages.summary: Learn to turn positions, ranges and a single pass into useful answers.

modules.title: 1. Read and change a sequence
modules.text: Practice zero-based indices, traversal, updating an element and slicing. Distinguish an index from the value stored there. Draw a five-cell array before touching code.

modules.title: 2. Keep useful information while scanning
modules.text: Track a minimum, maximum, running sum or frequency map. State exactly what your variables summarize after processing the first i elements.

modules.title: 3. Introduce range patterns
modules.text: Build prefix sums for repeated range totals. Then use two pointers on sorted data and a fixed-size sliding window. Variable-size windows need a condition that can be maintained correctly; revisit them with strings.

exercises.title: Move zeroes
exercises.prompt: Move all zeroes to the end while preserving the order of nonzero values. Try an in-place write pointer.
exercises.hint: Where should the next nonzero value be written?

exercises.title: Range totals
exercises.prompt: Build prefix sums, then answer inclusive index-range sum queries.
exercises.hint: Use a prefix array starting with zero; subtract two prefix entries.

checks: Explain why one forward scan is sufficient for moving zeroes.
Answer a range query without scanning its range again.
pitfalls: Slicing copies data; it can quietly add time and memory.
Do not assume a positive-number sliding-window proof still works when negatives are allowed.
stages.complexity: A Python list is a dynamic array: indexed access is O(1); append is amortized O(1), although a resizing append can be O(n). Middle insertion/deletion and linear search are O(n). Prefix preprocessing is O(n); each range query is O(1).

stages.title: Strings
stages.summary: Treat text as a sequence, while being explicit about what counts as a character.

modules.title: 1. Establish the text rules
modules.text: Practice indexing, splitting, joining and parsing. Decide whether case, spaces and punctuation matter before solving a text problem.

modules.title: 2. Count and compare
modules.text: Use character frequencies to test anagrams. Use two pointers for palindromes, and compare this with reversing the entire string.

modules.title: 3. Grow and shrink a window
modules.text: Find the longest substring without repeated characters using a set or last-seen dictionary. Explain why the left boundary never moves backward. Save rolling hashes and advanced pattern matching for later.

exercises.title: Anagram test
exercises.prompt: For lowercase English letters, decide whether two strings have the same character counts.
exercises.hint: Compare frequencies, not just sets.

exercises.title: Longest unique substring
exercises.prompt: Return the length of the longest substring containing no repeated code point.
exercises.hint: When a repeat arrives, move the left boundary only as far forward as necessary.

checks: Distinguish substring from subsequence.
Explain why both boundaries together move at most O(n) times.
pitfalls: Python strings are immutable. Repeatedly building longer strings by concatenation can be quadratic; collect pieces and join.
Python str indexes Unicode code points, which are not always user-perceived characters. Normalization and grapheme-aware processing are separate requirements; do not silently assume ASCII.
stages.complexity: A linear scan is O(n) in the number of code points. Frequency-map space depends on the number of distinct symbols. Comparing or copying a length-k substring can cost O(k).

stages.title: Linked lists
stages.summary: Practice changing connections without losing the rest of the structure.

modules.title: 1. Draw nodes and references
modules.text: Build a small Node class with value and next fields. Traverse from the head until None. A Python list is not a linked list.

modules.title: 2. Rewire carefully
modules.text: Insert at the head, remove after a known predecessor and reverse a singly linked list. Save the next reference before overwriting it; use a dummy head when it simplifies boundary cases.

modules.title: 3. Compare list variants
modules.text: Understand previous links in a doubly linked list and the stopping rule in a circular list. Then try slow/fast pointers for finding the middle or detecting a cycle.

exercises.title: Reverse a list
exercises.prompt: Return the new head after reversing every next link.
exercises.hint: Maintain previous, current and saved-next references.

exercises.title: Detect a cycle
exercises.prompt: Return whether repeatedly following next can revisit a node.
exercises.example: A → B → C → B gives True; A → B → None gives False
exercises.hint: Compare node identity, not equal values.

checks: Reverse an empty list and a single-node list safely.
Explain why two nodes with the same value need not be the same node.
pitfalls: Finding the node still takes time. “Linked-list insertion is O(1)” only applies when the necessary node/reference is already known.
Deleting a singly linked node normally requires its predecessor; do not generalize a special trick to all cases.
stages.complexity: Search and access by index are O(n). Head insertion is O(1). Iterative reversal is O(n) time with O(1) extra space. Doubly linked lists spend additional space on previous references.

stages.title: Stack & queue
stages.summary: Choose the next item by arrival order or by most recent use.

modules.title: 1. Use the two interfaces
modules.text: A stack is last-in, first-out; a queue is first-in, first-out. Trace push/pop and enqueue/dequeue by hand before implementing either.

modules.title: 2. Pick Python containers
modules.text: Use list.append/pop for a stack and collections.deque with append/popleft for a queue. Handle removal from an empty container deliberately.

modules.title: 3. Apply and revisit
modules.text: Use stacks for matching brackets and queues for ordered processing. After the basics, revisit monotonic stacks with next-greater-element problems and deques with sliding-window maxima; they are extensions, not entry requirements.

exercises.title: Balanced brackets
exercises.prompt: Accept (), [] and {} only; return whether nesting is valid.
exercises.hint: Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opener.

exercises.title: Queue with two stacks
exercises.prompt: Implement enqueue and dequeue using an input and an output stack.
exercises.hint: Move items only when the output stack is empty.

checks: Explain why a queue is needed for level-by-level processing.
Show why each item in a two-stack queue is transferred at most once.
pitfalls: Python list.pop(0) shifts remaining elements and is O(n).
A monotonic stack may contain a nested while loop yet still do O(n) total pushes and pops.
stages.complexity: List stack operations at the end are amortized O(1); deque endpoint operations are O(1). A two-stack queue has amortized O(1) operations, although one dequeue can trigger O(n) work.

stages.title: Recursion
stages.summary: Solve a smaller version of the same problem, then combine the result.

modules.title: 1. Name the contract and base case
modules.text: Say what one function call returns. Choose a base case and a measure that gets smaller on every recursive step. Trace calls and returns separately.

modules.title: 2. Understand the call stack
modules.text: Record each call’s parameters and local variables. Rewrite a simple recursive traversal iteratively to see what an explicit stack replaces.

modules.title: 3. Add divide-and-conquer, then choices
modules.text: Implement merge sort after understanding its merge step. Introduce backtracking with subsets: choose, explore, undo. Revisit harder backtracking after tree traversals rather than blocking progress here.

exercises.title: Recursive sum
exercises.prompt: Sum a list by advancing an index rather than slicing the remainder.
exercises.hint: The index reaching len(values) is the base case.

exercises.title: All subsets
exercises.prompt: Produce each subset of distinct input values exactly once.
exercises.hint: For each value, decide whether to include it.

checks: Explain both why your recursion terminates and why it returns the right result.
Identify the maximum call depth and count the number of generated results.
pitfalls: Recursion is not automatically efficient: repeated subproblems can multiply work.
Python has a recursion-depth limit; prefer iterative traversal for potentially very deep inputs.
stages.complexity: Recursive indexed summation uses O(n) time and O(n) call-stack space. Materializing all subsets needs Θ(n·2ⁿ) total output space/time in the usual list representation; recursion depth alone is only O(n).

stages.title: Binary search
stages.summary: Discard half the possibilities using a condition that changes in one direction.

modules.title: 1. Search sorted data
modules.text: Start with ascending arrays and an explicit interval convention. Trace empty, one-item and missing-target cases. Never mix inclusive and half-open bounds.

modules.title: 2. Find boundaries, not just equality
modules.text: Implement the first index with value ≥ target, then the first with value > target. Use these boundaries to count duplicates.

modules.title: 3. Search an answer space
modules.text: Try integer square root, then a feasibility problem. Prove that the predicate is monotonic: once true, it remains true, or vice versa. A large search space alone does not justify binary search.

exercises.title: First occurrence
exercises.prompt: Return the leftmost index of a target, or -1 if absent.
exercises.hint: Find the lower bound, then verify equality.

exercises.title: Integer square root
exercises.prompt: For a nonnegative integer x, return the largest integer r with r*r ≤ x.
exercises.hint: Keep track of which side contains feasible candidates.

checks: State what your search interval still contains after each iteration.
Prove that every iteration makes the interval smaller.
pitfalls: Searching unsorted data with ordinary binary search is invalid.
bisect returns an insertion position, which does not prove the value exists.
stages.complexity: Binary search uses O(log n) comparisons on a random-access array. If a feasibility check costs C, answer-space search costs O(C log R) for R candidate values. Inserting into a Python list after bisect still costs O(n).

code.title: A reusable lower-bound search
code.explanation: Precondition: values is sorted in ascending order. All positions before lo are too small; positions at or after hi are valid lower-bound candidates. The result may equal len(values).

stages.title: Trees
stages.summary: Use recursive structure to organize hierarchical information.

modules.title: 1. Learn the shape
modules.text: Define root, child, leaf, depth and height. Distinguish a general tree, a binary tree and a binary search tree (BST); they are different promises.

modules.title: 2. Traverse systematically
modules.text: Implement preorder, inorder and postorder DFS, then level-order BFS with a queue. Choose the order based on when the parent needs its children’s results.

modules.title: 3. Maintain search order
modules.text: Search and insert in a BST with an explicit duplicate policy. Validate using inherited lower/upper bounds, then learn why balanced trees maintain short paths. Rotations can be a later study.

exercises.title: Maximum depth
exercises.prompt: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path; an empty tree has depth zero.
exercises.hint: Combine child depths after recursive calls return.

exercises.title: Validate a BST
exercises.prompt: Assume distinct keys. Check that every node satisfies all ancestor bounds.
exercises.example: Root 10, right child 15, and 15’s left child 6 → False
exercises.hint: Checking only immediate parent–child pairs misses this violation.

checks: Explain why inorder traversal of a valid BST produces sorted keys.
Choose DFS or BFS and account for its memory on a narrow versus wide tree.
pitfalls: A binary tree is not necessarily a BST.
BST operations are O(height), not unconditionally O(log n); sorted insertion can create a chain.
stages.complexity: A full traversal visits n nodes in O(n) time. Recursive DFS uses O(h) stack space. BFS uses O(w) queue space for maximum width w. A balanced BST has O(log n) height; an unbalanced one may have O(n).

stages.title: Heap
stages.summary: Keep the next highest-priority item easy to retrieve.

modules.title: 1. Separate heap order from sorted order
modules.text: A min-heap puts the smallest value at the root; it does not sort siblings or the entire array. Learn the array positions of parents and children.

modules.title: 2. Maintain the invariant
modules.text: Trace sift-up after insertion and sift-down after removal. Use heapq.heapify, heappush and heappop in Python. For broadly compatible max-priority numeric examples, store negative priorities.

modules.title: 3. Keep only what matters
modules.text: Maintain a heap of size k for the k largest values. Add a tie-break counter when priority entries contain tasks that cannot be compared directly.

exercises.title: Kth largest
exercises.prompt: Return the kth largest value, counting duplicates, for 1 ≤ k ≤ n.
exercises.hint: Keep a min-heap containing only the largest k values seen.

exercises.title: Merge sorted streams
exercises.prompt: Merge several already-sorted lists into one sorted result.
exercises.hint: The heap needs only the next available item from each stream.

checks: Explain why the root of a size-k min-heap is the kth largest retained value.
Distinguish a priority queue’s behavior from its heap implementation.
pitfalls: The heap’s internal list is not globally sorted.
Validate k; decide how empty input and priority ties should behave.
stages.complexity: Peek is O(1); push/pop are O(log n); bottom-up heapify is O(n). Keeping the top k uses O(n log k) time for k ≥ 2 and O(k) space; k = 1 is a linear scan.

stages.title: Graphs
stages.summary: Model connections first, then choose a traversal or path algorithm.

modules.title: 1. Represent the problem
modules.text: Identify vertices, edges, direction and weights. Build an adjacency list; contrast its storage with an adjacency matrix. Include disconnected vertices.

modules.title: 2. Traverse and remember
modules.text: Use BFS for minimum edge-count paths in an unweighted graph, and DFS for exploration and components. Mark visited vertices at discovery so cycles do not create repeated work.

modules.title: 3. Respect algorithm conditions
modules.text: Learn topological sorting for directed acyclic graphs. Then use a heap-based Dijkstra implementation for nonnegative edge weights. Negative edges need another method, such as Bellman–Ford.

modules.title: 4. Revisit spanning trees
modules.text: After union–find in the optional stage, try Kruskal; after heaps, try Prim. A minimum spanning tree connects an undirected weighted graph cheaply and solves a different problem from shortest paths.

exercises.title: Fewest hops
exercises.prompt: Find the minimum number of edges from A to D, or report unreachable.
exercises.hint: BFS discovers vertices in increasing distance layers.

exercises.title: Course dependencies
exercises.prompt: Return a valid order of courses from prerequisite edges, or report a cycle.
exercises.example: A → C, B → C → either A,B,C or B,A,C
exercises.hint: Repeatedly remove a vertex whose remaining indegree is zero.

checks: Explain why ordinary BFS fails for arbitrary unequal edge weights.
Test a disconnected graph, a cycle and a single isolated vertex.
pitfalls: An undirected edge normally belongs in both adjacency lists.
Dijkstra requires nonnegative weights; a visited-set shortcut copied from BFS is not a substitute for understanding relaxation.
stages.complexity: With adjacency lists, BFS/DFS run in O(V + E) time and use O(V) auxiliary state beyond graph storage. Binary-heap Dijkstra is commonly O((V + E) log V) on simple graphs; duplicate heap entries and graph representation affect the precise bound.

stages.title: Dynamic programming
stages.summary: Reuse solutions to precisely defined subproblems.

modules.title: 1. Define the state in a sentence
modules.text: Before writing a table, say what dp[i] or dp[i][j] means. Identify which information must be remembered so the next decision is valid.

modules.title: 2. Write transitions and base cases
modules.text: List the choices that produce each state, then specify starting and impossible states. Write a small recursive version to expose repeated work.

modules.title: 3. Cache, order, then optimize
modules.text: Add memoization, or compute bottom-up in dependency order. Explain where the final answer lives. Only compress space after the full table is correct and you understand which old states are still needed.

exercises.title: Climbing stairs
exercises.prompt: Count ways to reach step n using moves of one or two steps. Define one way to reach step zero: take no steps.
exercises.hint: ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2].

exercises.title: Minimum coins
exercises.prompt: Given positive coin denominations usable repeatedly, find the fewest coins for an amount, or -1 if impossible.
exercises.hint: Greedily taking the largest coin first gives the wrong answer here.

checks: State the meaning, transition, base cases, evaluation order and final answer without looking at code.
Explain the number of states multiplied by work per state.
pitfalls: Memoization only helps when identical states recur; include every relevant variable in the cache key.
Coin-change O(amount × coin types) depends on the numeric amount, not merely its bit length; it is pseudopolynomial.
stages.complexity: Stairs uses O(n) arithmetic operations and can use O(1) stored states. Exact counts grow, so big-integer arithmetic is not truly constant-cost for arbitrarily large n. A full coin table uses O(amount) space.

code.title: Start with an explicit DP table
code.explanation: Contract: n is a nonnegative integer. ways[step] counts all valid move sequences ending at that step. The final move was either one or two steps, so the two cases are disjoint.

stages.title: Advanced topics
stages.summary: Choose a branch that supports the problems you actually want to solve.

modules.title: 1. Tries for prefixes
modules.text: After strings and trees, implement insert, whole-word lookup and prefix lookup. Mark word endings separately so “car” and “cart” can coexist.

modules.title: 2. Union–find for connectivity
modules.text: After graphs, learn find and union with path compression and union by size/rank. Apply it to incremental connectivity and Kruskal’s minimum spanning tree algorithm.

modules.title: 3. Range-query structures
modules.text: After prefix sums and trees, learn a Fenwick tree for prefix sums with updates, or a segment tree for range aggregates. Define the combine operation and identity before implementation.

modules.title: 4. Bitmasks and specialized algorithms
modules.text: After subsets and DP, represent small sets with bits and try subset DP. Pick advanced string algorithms, greedy proofs or further graph algorithms only when a concrete problem motivates them.

exercises.title: Prefix dictionary
exercises.prompt: Insert car, cart and dog; distinguish a whole word from a prefix.
exercises.hint: A path existing is not the same as an end-of-word marker.

exercises.title: Online connectivity
exercises.prompt: Start with vertices 0–3, then union(0,1) and union(2,3). Query, merge, and query again.
exercises.hint: Compare representatives rather than direct parent pointers.

checks: Explain why the specialized structure is preferable to a simpler baseline.
Complete one chosen branch thoroughly before collecting several unfamiliar templates.
pitfalls: Advanced does not mean universally better: implementation complexity and memory can outweigh benefits.
Bitmask enumeration is exponential in the number of represented elements; keep that universe small.
stages.complexity: Trie lookup is O(L) with constant-time child access assumptions. Union–find with both optimizations has near-constant amortized cost O(α(n)). Standard segment-tree point updates and range queries are O(log n); build is O(n).
